s: You're listening to Short Wave from NPR.
你正在听NPR的短波。
Emily Kwong
Hey, Short Wavers, Emily Kwong here.
快浪者，艾米丽·昆。
Now, with Thanksgiving just around the corner, I come to you with a story about turkeys and how one man devoted his scientific career to protecting them.
现在，感恩节即将到来，我告诉你一个关于火的故事，以及一个人如何把科学生涯献给保护它们。
This man, his name is Mike Chamberlain, and he grew up in Central Virginia.
这个人，他的名字是迈克·钱伯莱恩，他在弗吉尼亚州中部长大。
My dad was an avid hunter.
我父亲是一位热情的猎人。
Mike Chamberlain
And so I became a hunter, basically, to spend time with my dad.
所以我成为一名猎人，基本上，为了和爸爸在一起。
I mean, what little boy doesn't want to be around his dad?
我的意思是，哪个小男孩不想和他的父亲在一起？
And as Mike got older, he started to hunt turkeys on his own every chance he got.
随着迈克的成长，他开始每次有机会独自猎。
Kwong
Me and my buddies, we would hunt during the week before school.
在学校前一周，我和我的朋友们会狩猎。
Chamberlain
We would hunt during the week after school.
我们在上学后的一周中会狩猎。
We would hunt on the weekends.
我们在周末会狩猎。
I can distinctly recall walking into first period government class and being in full camouflage because I had rushed out of the field and gotten to school just in time.
我清楚地记得走进了第一阶段的政府班，在完全伪装中，因为我赶上了场，在学校的时间上班。
The whole experience captivated Mike.
整个经历吸引了迈克。
Kwong
The birds are singing.
鸟儿正在唱歌。
Chamberlain
And in the case of wild turkeys, the males are gobbling.
对于野生来说，雄性动物正在吞。
They're displaying.
他们正在展示。
And it just became really attractive to me.
这让我变得非常有吸引力。
It became part of who I was.
它成为了我的一部分。
And then, when I ultimately got the opportunity to study turkeys, there was a kind of a natural conduit from being a turkey hunter to then becoming a turkey scientist.
然后，当我终于有机会学习子时，从猎人到科学家的自然通道出现了。
These days, Mike is the National Wild Turkey Federation Distinguished Professor at the University of Georgia, where his job is to study wild turkeys.
今天，迈克是格鲁吉亚大学国家野生土耳其联合会的杰出教授，他的工作是研究野生。
Kwong
And wild turkeys, they are the same species as domesticated turkeys.
野生是同家禽一样的物种。
They just look a little different.
他们只是看起来有点不同。
The wild turkey that lives in our environments, they are much smaller, largely dark-colored and iridescent.
在我们的环境中生活的野生，它们更小，主要是黑色和色。
Chamberlain
That shininess attracts attention from females.
这种光泽吸引了女性的注意。
They have pronounced flocks and pronounced sociality.
他们表达了群群，表达了社交。
And their behaviors are quite complex.
他们的行为非常复杂。
Mike's experiences hunting, of being close to these birds, of going to the places where they roost in the wild, is something he's carried into his work as a scientist.
迈克的狩猎经历，接近这些鸟类，在野外放浪的地方，是他作为科学家的工作中所带来的东西。
Kwong

Hunting the bird and spending time in their environment, where you're the guest and they are doing things that they've been wired for millennia to do, that offers you a very different perspective that is complementary, I think, to the science that I do because it gives me a lens into their behavior that I would otherwise not have.
狩猎鸟，在它们的环境中度过时间，在这里，你是客人，他们做了几千年来一直在做的事情，这提供了一个非常不同的视角，我认为，我所做的科学是因为它给了我对他们的行为的镜头。
Chamberlain
And over three decades of studying these birds, both in the wild and through data, Mike has started to notice a pattern, one that's worrying him.
在研究这些鸟类的30多年里，在自然环境中和通过数据，迈克开始注意到一个模式，一个让他担心。
Kwong
Around 2010, we started documenting and reporting what appeared to be fairly widespread population declines.
在2010年左右，我们开始记录和报告似乎相当普遍的人口下降。
Chamberlain
And now, fast-forward to 2026.
现在，快速前进到2026年。
Those declines have been documented throughout broad areas of the species range.
这些减少已被记录在物种范围广泛的地区。

So today on the show, the fight for the American wild turkey, what's driving their population decline in the southeastern US, what conservation efforts have looked like in the past, and what they could look like in the future.
所以今天在节目中，为了美国野生而战，在美国东南部，过去的保护工作是什么样子，在未来，它们可能会是什么样子。
Kwong
I'm Emily Kwong.
我的名字是艾米丽·昆。
And you're listening to Short Wave, the science podcast from NPR.
你正在听NPR的科学播客"短波".
Talking about how, in some parts of the country, we're seeing a decline in wild turkeys.
谈到一些地方，野生的数量正在下降。
But this is not the first time.
但这不是第一次。
In fact, in the 1930s, wild turkeys almost went extinct.
事实上，在20世纪30年代，野生几乎灭绝了。
But there was a massive conservation effort to save them.
但为了拯救它们，进行了大量的保护工作。
How did that happen?
这怎么发生了？
Like, what went into turning the almost turkey extinction around?
比如，什么导致了几乎的灭绝？
Yeah, I mean, wild turkeys have followed a well-publicized kind of trajectory through time.
是的，我的意思是，野已经遵循了广告的时间轨迹。
Chamberlain
You know, basically, you had a group of state wildlife biologists across the east and southeast that were turkey hunters at heart.
你知道的，基本上，你在东部和东南地区有一群州野生生物学家，
And they were dismayed at the fact that wild turkeys had largely disappeared from most of the landscape.
他们感到震惊的是，野生已经从大部分地区消失了。
And so they started seeking ways of trying to restore the wild turkey to the landscape.
所以他们开始寻找方法，
And some of those early efforts failed, largely because they-- they tried to use game farm birds or domestic birds and release them.
一些早期的努力失败了，主要是因为他们试图利用狩猎农场鸟类或家禽释放它们。
That was a colossal failure.
这是一个巨大的失败。

But then, in the 1950s, '60s, '70s, '80s, and even into the 1990s, you started seeing widespread population recovery, which was largely attributable to state agencies capturing wild turkeys and translocating them and releasing them to restore populations.
但在20世纪50年代，六十年代，七十年代，八十年代，甚至到九十年代，你开始看到广泛的人口复苏，这主要归因于国家机构捕获野生，转移它们并释放它们以恢复种群。
States started collaborating together to move turkeys across state lines.
各国开始合作，移动子穿越州界限。
And that's when restoration really, really accelerated.
这就是恢复真正的加速时。
And I suppose you were the beneficiary of that as a young person because that's when you started turkey hunting.
我猜你作为一个年轻人受益了，因为那时你开始狩猎。
Kwong
I was.
我是。
Chamberlain
Exactly.
确切的。
I can remember, as a child, seeing a turkey while hunting, and--
我记得，作为一个孩子，看到一个在狩猎，
Yeah?
是的？
Kwong
--it was like you had struck the lottery.
--就像你打了彩票一样。
Chamberlain
And then, in the mid and late 1980s, I can distinctly remember seeing the population start to increase in my local area--
在20世纪80年代中期和后期，我清楚地记得我在当地地区的人口开始增加。
Right.
很好。
Kwong
--where it wasn't uncommon to hear a bird.
在那里听到鸟儿并不罕见。
Chamberlain
It wasn't uncommon to see a bird.
看到鸟并不罕见。
And then I can remember the 1990s as a hunter, just thinking--
然后我记得90年代作为一个猎人，
Yeah.
是的，是的。
Kwong
--there are turkeys everywhere.
Chamberlain
Right, until they started declining.
直到它们开始下降。
Kwong
Yes, and hunters like myself were the first to really start seeing those declines because we could see it in our local populations that we had been-- that we had been hunting for years.
是的，像我这样的猎人是第一个真正开始看到这些下降的，因为我们可以看到在我们的当地人口，
Chamberlain
Let's talk about some of the decline we're seeing of wild turkeys in the southeastern US.
让我们谈谈美国东南部野生的下降。
Kwong
What are some of the reasons that's happening?
这发生的原因是什么？
I think it's really three habitat components that are all linked together.
我认为这实际上是三个生息地组成部分，
Chamberlain
One, if you just look around the southeastern United States, just evaluate with your own eyes what's changed in the last 10 or 15 or 20 years.
首先，如果你只看看美国东南部，用自己的眼睛评估过去10或15或20年发生了什么变化。
I think most of us would agree that there have been dramatic losses in habitat to urbanization, suburban development.
我认为我们大多数人都会同意，城市化，郊区发展造成了巨大息地损失。
And so habitat loss is a major issue.
因此，生息地丧失是一个重大问题。
We are also seeing habitat fragmentation be problematic, that you take chunks of habitat and split them up into smaller and smaller pieces of habitat.
我们也看到息地碎片化是个问题，它们被分成越来越小的生息地。
Wow, yeah.
，是的。
Kwong
Things that would exacerbate that issue, such as highways, power rights of way, roads, that may seem somewhat bizarre for a bird that can fly, that that fragmentation would be an issue.
那些会加剧这个问题，如高速公路，电力通行权，对于可以飞行的鸟类来说，这可能看起来有些奇怪，这种分裂将成为一个问题。
Chamberlain
Don't they just fly across it?
他们不会飞过它吗？
And the answer is, well, they can just fly across it, but we have data clearly showing that in many cases, they do not.
答案是，它们可以飞过它，但我们有数据清楚地表明，在许多情况下，它们不会。
They perceive these barriers as true barriers to movement.
他们认为这些障碍是真正的障碍。
And so that's a second habitat issue.
所以这是第二个息地问题。
And the third would just be degradation.
而第三个只是降解。
The quality of the habitat?
环境的质量？
Kwong
Yeah, just the changes to how habitat is maintained.
是的，只是环境的变化。
Chamberlain
There have been dramatic declines in the use of prescribed fire, which is a real benefit for the wild turkey because prescribed fire takes dense vegetation and converts it back--
这对野生来说是个真正的好处，因为预定的火把密集的植被带回了--
Mm-hmm, OK.
，好吧。
Kwong
--to open vegetation that turkeys can see through and navigate through.
打开可以看到的植被，
Chamberlain
All of their day is spent from your waist to your toes.
他们的整天都是从你的腰部到你的脚。
When they're walking around, when they're trying to forage, when they're trying to avoid predators, all of that's occurring--
当他们走路，当他们试图寻找食物，当他们试图避免掠食者，所有这些都发生--
Aw.
，这是一个问题。
Kwong
--around your knee, because that's where their head is, right?
它们的头部在你的膝盖上，对吧？
Chamberlain
And so--
所以--
They're too short.
他们太短了。
Kwong
--if you think about it, their ability to survive, to avoid predators, hinges on the ability--
它们的生存能力，避免掠食者，取决于它们的能力。
Chamberlain
Yeah.
是的，是的。
Kwong
--to be able to see at the level of your knee, or at most, your thigh.
在你的膝盖水平，或者最多，你的大腿水平。
Chamberlain
And so, as we've seen these declines in the use of fire, we have seen a predictable degradation in habitat fall.
随着使用火的下降，我们看到了预测性地息地衰退。
And it kind of makes sense, honestly, if you think about these burns are--
坦率地说，如果你想到这些烧伤是...
Kwong
Yes, yes.
是的，是的。
Chamberlain
--a natural thing that, prior to humans, would happen because of, like, lightning and stuff.
在人类之前，由于闪电等事情而发生的自然事物。
Kwong
Sure.
当然。
Chamberlain
So, besides habitat loss, habitat fragmentation, and habitat degradation, is there anything else that's a threat to wild turkeys in the southeast?
除了息地丧失，息地碎片化和息地退化之外，还有什么威胁到东南部的野生吗？
Kwong
There are a number of factors that go into influencing kind of the outcome of a wild turkey population from one year to the next.
许多因素会影响野生火种群的一年到一年的结果。
Chamberlain
I kind of liken it to a football game.
我把它比如足球比赛。
OK.
没有问题。
Kwong
So, imagine every football game is a year.
所以，想象每场足球比赛都是一年。
Chamberlain
Everybody that's a football fan knows that there are positions on the field that influence--
每个是足球球迷都知道，球场上有影响...
Yeah.
是的，是的。
Kwong
--every game-- the offensive line--
每场比赛-- 进攻线--
Chamberlain
Yeah.
是的，是的。
Kwong
--the defensive line, and the quarterback.
防守线和后卫。
Chamberlain
Those are the big things, like habitat, that influence every game.
这就是大物，如息地，影响每一种游戏。
But there are certain positions on the field that may influence one game and not the next game.
但在场上有某些位置可能影响一场比赛而不是下一场比赛。
Yeah.
是的，是的。
Kwong
You could have disease issues that are affecting a population of turkeys in your area, but it doesn't affect the population of turkeys in the next county over.
你可能会患有影响到你所在地区的种群的疾病，但它不会影响下一个县的火种群。
Chamberlain
You could have situations where predator communities are having a disproportionate impact on turkeys in a certain area, but not in a different area.
你可能会遇到特定地区的捕食者群体对土耳其产生不成比例的影响，但不是在另一个地区。
You can have scenarios where the impacts of hunting are more pronounced in one game than in another game.
狩猎的影响在一个游戏中比在另一个游戏更明显的场景。

And so, because each outcome could be different, and each position could influence the outcome differently from one place in North America to the next, it creates a very complex set of questions that prompts research, like what I do, to try to provide data across the species range.
所以，因为每个结果可能是不同的，每个位置都会在北美不同的地方影响结果，它创造了一个非常复杂的问题集，像我这样做，试图提供物种范围内的数据。
All the big things and all the little things can add up to decide an outcome.
所有的大事和小事都能结合在一起决定结果。
Kwong
Yes.
是的，是的。
Chamberlain
I'm wondering, so if the health of a turkey population is a football game, how can we ensure it comes out, like, team turkey?
我想知道，如果土耳其人口的健康是足球比赛，我们怎么能保证它能出现在球队？。
Kwong
What needs to be done in science, and what do regular people need to do?
科学需要做些什么，普通人需要做些什么？

Yeah, from a scientific perspective, I think that the future of the wild turkey is going to hinge on the ability of people like me to conduct rigorous science that is iterative and is able to adjust as landscape conditions change, as society changes.
从科学角度来看，我认为野生的未来将取决于像我这样的人进行严格的科学的能力。
Chamberlain

And I think, from a societal perspective, the future of the wild turkey is going to hinge on the willingness of private landowners to prioritize this bird and, more importantly, the places where it thrives.
我认为，从社会角度来看，野生的未来将取决于私人土地所有者愿意优先考虑这只鸟，更重要的是，它繁荣的地方。
We're going to have to prioritize those areas and conserve them and manage them appropriately because the future of the bird is going to hinge on the conservation and management of those birds.
我们必须优先考虑这些区域，保护它们，并适当管理它们，因为鸟类的未来将取决于保护和管理这些鸟类。
And for folks who aren't, perhaps, property owners, but who want to help wild turkeys, what would you suggest they do?
对于那些不是房地产所有者，但希望帮助野生子的人来说，你建议他们做什么？
Kwong
So one thing you can do, I mean, if you-- if you're observing wild turkeys and you're in your local area, is just download an app like iNaturalist or something on your phone--
所以你可以做的一件事，如果你在当地观察野生，只是在你的手机上下载一款像Inaturalist这样的应用程序
Chamberlain
Mm, I love that app.
我喜欢那个应用程序。
Kwong
Yeah.
是的，是的。
--and input the data when you see--
--当你看到--
Chamberlain
OK.
没有问题。
Kwong
--turkeys.
Chamberlain

If you're more interested in my specific research and being a part of that, one of the projects that we started two years ago, which is called Wild Turkey DNA, it involves the cooperation of-- of hunters who take a tissue sample from the bird and put it in a vial with a solution in it that we send them with a postage paid kit.
如果你更感兴趣的是我的研究，一个我们两年前开始的项目，它被称为野生土耳其DNA，它涉及到狩猎者合作，他们从鸟儿中取出一个组织样本。
And they put the sample in the vial, put it in the freezer, and then drop it in the mail, and it comes back to us.
他们把样本放到瓶子里，把它放进冰箱里，然后把它放到邮箱里，它回到了我们身边。
And we use that tissue sample--
我们用那种组织样本--
Wow.
，这是个好事。
Kwong
--to conduct genetic analyses.
为了进行遗传分析。
Chamberlain
And from that sample, we can determine where the bird originated from.
根据这个样本，我们可以确定这只鸟来自哪里。
We can look at patterns of genetic diversity.
我们可以研究遗传多样性的模式。
We can--
我们可以--
Wow.
，这是个好事。
Kwong
--look at inbreeding levels.
Chamberlain
We can evaluate gene flow across the landscape.
我们可以评估整个景观的基因流动。
We've sampled over 2,000 birds so far.
到目前为止，我们已经抽取了2000多只鸟类。
If that's something that you're interested in, you can actually go to wildturkeydna.com and look at the results that we're posting.
如果你有兴趣的话，你可以去 wildturkeydna.com，看看我们发布的结果。
Mike Chamberlain, thank you so much for coming on Short Wave to talk about this incredible bird and what you all are trying to do as scientists to support them.
迈克·钱伯莱恩，谢谢你们来到短浪节目中，来谈论这个令人难以置信的鸟类，以及你们作为科学家，
Kwong
Oh, it was so good to join you.
很高兴能加入你。
Chamberlain
I appreciate the opportunity to-- to share a little conversation about the wild turkey.
我很欣赏有机会分享一些关于野生的谈话。
Me, too.
我也是。
Kwong
And happy Thanksgiving to you.
祝你一个快乐的感恩节。
Same to you.
你也是如此。
Chamberlain
As we wrap up the show, I have an invitation for you.
当我们结束节目，我有一个邀请给你。
Kwong
If you've ever been curious to see what we do here at NPR headquarters in person, you're going to love this.
如果您曾经想知道我们在NPR总部亲自做什么，您会喜欢这个。
You are the public in public media, and now you can enter for a chance to go behind the scenes at NPR.
你是公众媒体的公众，现在你可以进入NPR的幕后。
One lucky winner will tour our building in Washington, DC, watch a live taping of All Things Considered, and have lunch with an NPR journalist.
一位幸运的获胜者将参观华盛顿特区的我们的建筑，观看"考虑一切"的现场录像，和NPR记者一起吃午饭。

在 npr.org/giveaway上可以免费访问。

当你进入网站时，您可以捐赠更多作品，并在此期间支持NPR网络。

你必须18岁或以上。

您可以在npr.org/giveaway找到入口页面和官方规则的链接。
